Du kennst das vielleicht. Der erste Gedanke am Morgen, noch bevor die Augen offen sind: nicht schon wieder ein Tag. Eine Erschöpfung, die kein Schlaf nimmt. data.copy:
The drug my own neurologist gave me for migraines made my family think I had Alzheimer's.

I was 60. I had been a nurse for 35 years. I have charted cognitive decline in other people's parents more times than I can count.

And I sat at my own kitchen table forgetting words, while the people who love me quietly started watching me the way you watch a patient.

I want to be precise about this, because precise is what I am. The drug was a preventive. A standard one. The kind I have seen on a hundred discharge sheets. And it did cut my migraine days, it did, I am not going to pretend it did nothing. But somewhere in month 3 I started losing nouns. The word for the thing you strain pasta with. The name of the street I grew up on. I would be mid-sentence and the sentence would just... stop, and everyone at the table would wait, and I would feel them waiting.

It got into the job too. I caught myself in the staff bathroom one afternoon, both hands on the sink, trying to remember the dose of a medication I have given out for 30 years. A drug I could have named in my sleep. I stood there until it came back. Then I dried my hands and went and gave report like nothing had happened, because that is what you do.

I have run cognitive screens on patients. I know the questions. What year is it. Count backward from a hundred by sevens. And it never once occurred to me to ask myself.

My husband called my sister about it before he called me. That is the part I keep coming back to. He noticed before I did. Me. The one who notices.

He told me later he had started writing things down. Dates. Little observations. He was charting me. My own husband had a chart on me and I never saw it, and I am the person who teaches new grads how to chart.

I went back to my neurologist and told him. He was kind about it. He lowered the dose. The fog cleared in a few weeks, slow, like coming up out of water. And the migraine days came right back to where they had been.

That preventive was not the firs…

I need to share this because I just did the math on my Pom and I'm honestly embarrassed.

$93.47 a month.

That's what I was spending on my Pomeranian's breathing. Ninety-three dollars and forty-seven cents every single month on products designed for dogs eight times her size.

Bella is 5 pounds. Eight years old. She has been my shadow since the day I brought her home. I would do anything for this dog. ANYTHING.

And that's the problem. Because "anything" turned into "everything I could find at the pet store" without ever asking whether any of it was right for her.

Let me break down what I was buying.

Product one: tracheal support chews from Amazon. $34 a month. The bag said "for dogs under 25 lbs." Bella weighs five pounds. A 24 lb dog is also "under 25 lbs." Those two dogs have nothing in common when it comes to airway health. But sure, same product, same dose.

I was breaking each chew into quarters with a pill cutter every morning, watching crumbs fall on the counter. Some days Bella probably got 30% of a chew. Some days 15%. I was guessing every single time.

Product two: airway drops from the vet. $28 a month. Bella hated them. She'd see that dropper bottle and bolt behind the couch. I'd pull her out, hold her mouth open, squirt it in, and half of it would end up on my shirt because she'd shake her little fox face.

Maybe she was getting half the dose. Maybe. And I was paying full price for the privilege of wrestling my dog every morning before coffee.

Product three: "calming" treats from the fancy pet store downtown. $31.47 a month. Supposed to reduce the breathing episodes by keeping her relaxed. Bella loved them. But they were treating the anxiety from the honking, not the actual tracheal problem. Like putting a band-aid on a broken pipe.

Three products. $93.47 a month. $1,121.64 a year. And my dog was still honking.

data.copy:
Three Yorkies in 19 years. I watched all three of them slowly stop breathing.

The first one, I thought was just old age. The second one, I blamed myself. The third one, I finally understood what was actually happening.

My name is Diane. I am 56 years old. I live in Savannah, Georgia. I have owned Yorkies my entire adult life. My first was Ginger. My second was Pebbles. My third is Mabel.

Ginger lived to be 12. Pebbles made it to 10. Mabel is 7 and she is the reason I am writing this.

Let me tell you about Ginger first.

I got Ginger when I was 33. Five pounds of absolute attitude. She slept on my pillow. She rode in my purse. More personality in that tiny body than most people I've met.

Around age 6, Ginger started making a sound. A honking, goose-like noise when she got excited or drank water too fast. I asked my vet. He said, "Small dogs do that. It's just reverse sneezing. Totally normal."

So I ignored it.

By age 8, the honking was happening every day. Multiple times. She would cough after meals. She would wheeze at night. I brought it up again. Different vet this time. She said, "Sounds like it could be tracheal collapse. Very common in toy breeds. We can manage it with cough suppressants."

Manage it.

Ginger was on Hydrocodone for the last four years of her life. The coughing got worse every year. By age 11, she was having episodes that lasted 20 minutes where her whole body would seize up trying to pull air through her throat. I would hold her on the bathroom floor at 3 AM, rubbing her chest, talking to her, begging her to breathe.

She passed at 12. The vet said her trachea had collapsed significantly. Grade 4. Near-complete airway obstruction. Four years on cough suppressants and her trachea just kept flattening.

I grieved Ginger for six months before I got Pebbles.

Pebbles was different. Smaller. Quieter. More cautious. I told myself I would do everything right this time. Harness from day one. Never a collar. Kept her weight perfect. Limited excit…

Sixteen minutes.

That's how fast a seemingly healthy cat can go from normal to dying on your kitchen floor.

Sat down.

Willow had been deficient for months. Maybe even years.

Routine physical.

Dr. Patel walked in.

Young.

Maybe 36.

Laptop in hand.

"Mr. Bellamy."

Firm handshake.

All business.

data.caption: I felt like the worst cat mom alive.
data.copy:
I spent fourteen months waking up every single morning and doing the same thing before I put my feet on the floor.

I scanned the carpet.

Not because I wanted to. Because I had to. Because Miso had thrown up in the night again — or was about to — and I'd learned the hard way what it felt like to step in it in the dark.

My name is Sarah. I'm 34 and I live in Nashville with my cat Miso, a five-year-old tortoiseshell I adopted the second month of the pandemic. She has slept on my pillow every night since the day I brought her home. She is the reason my apartment doesn't feel empty.

She started throwing up when she was four.

Not hairballs. Not the occasional gag. Real vomiting. Three, four times a week. Sometimes every day. Undigested food on the kitchen tile at 6am. The wet sound from the other room at 2am that I'd learned to recognize in my sleep.

I took her to the vet three times in the first six months.

Three full exams. Three sets of bloodwork. All normal.

"Some cats just have sensitive stomachs," the third vet told me. "She's healthy. Try a different food."

I had already tried four different foods.

I tried a fifth. Then a sixth. I tried grain-free. I tried limited ingredient. I tried the $85 prescription diet the second vet recommended. I bought a slow feeder bowl. I bought an elevated dish. I tried a probiotic that cost $40 and lasted three weeks and did absolutely nothing.

Every single morning I woke up and scanned that carpet.

And every single morning that I found something — and most mornings I did — I felt like the worst cat mom alive.

Not because I hadn't tried. I had tried everything I could think of and everything three different vets had suggested. But she was still throwing up. And when you love something as much as I love Miso, "I tried" doesn't feel like enough when the answer still isn't working.

data.copy:
My own dog bit someone last year.

I'm a veterinarian. I've spent thirteen years treating dogs with behavioral conditions. I know every reactive dog protocol available.

I'd been managing my dog's reactivity with those protocols for two years.

She bit a jogger on our usual trail on a Tuesday morning in March.

The jogger was fine. Required a bandage. Didn't press charges.

I stood on that trail holding the lead, looking at what had just happened, and I could not find an explanation.

I had done everything I tell my clients to do.

Everything.

My name is Dr. Karen Patel, DVM. Along with Dr. Steven Reeves and Dr. Michelle Torres, I've spent the last thirteen years at Maplewood Animal Clinic treating dogs with anxiety, fear-based aggression, and leash reactivity. Between us, we've treated over 26,000 dogs.

My dog is a 4-year-old Border Collie named Rue.

I adopted her knowing she had a history of leash reactivity. I told myself I had an advantage — professional knowledge, access to the best protocols, relationships with the best trainers in our area.

I started working with a certified behaviorist within the first month.

Counter-conditioning. BAT protocol. Precise threshold management. Muzzle training as a safety layer. Prescription Trazodone when her baseline anxiety was particularly elevated.

For eighteen months, we made real progress.

Then she plateaued.

I added a second trainer. Different approach. Some improvement. Another plateau.

I tried every calming supplement I'd ever recommended to a client. The ones with the best reviews. The ones my colleagues mentioned at conferences. The "vet recommended" products I'd been suggesting for years.

Slight improvement. Nothing that held.

The inconsistency was what I couldn't explain professionally.

Some days Rue was almost normal. Same route, same conditions, same everything — she'd pass two dogs without reacting and I'd think we were finally breaking through.

Then the next day she'd explode at a dog 40 meters…

data.copy:
Your vet said "collapsing trachea, we'll manage it with cough suppressants."

And you drove home feeling relieved.

You filled the prescription. You adjusted the dosage. You kept him calm during episodes. You told yourself: we're managing this.

I need to tell you something that's going to be uncomfortable.

That relief you felt? That was the most dangerous moment of your Yorkie's life.

"Manage it with cough suppressants" sounds like a plan.

It is not a plan.

It is symptom silencing. Not cartilage support.

Let me explain.

My name is Dr. Michael Reeves. I'm a board-certified veterinary internal medicine specialist in Austin, Texas. 11 years of practice. I specialize in respiratory conditions in toy breeds.

I am not your regular vet. I am the person your vet refers you to when cough suppressants stop working and your Yorkie can't breathe.

I see Yorkies every single week. More than almost any other breed for tracheal collapse. They are among the most predisposed breeds for this condition. That is not opinion. That is published veterinary literature.

And almost every owner who walks through my door says the same thing:

"But we did everything right. We gave the cough suppressant. We used a harness. We kept the weight down."

I know you did.

That is not why you're here.

You're here because cough suppressants silence the honking. They do NOT rebuild the tracheal rings that are collapsing.

Hydrocodone manages the cough reflex. It does not repair cartilage.

Trazodone manages the anxiety during episodes. It does not strengthen the airway.

Between vet visits, nothing was happening to support the actual tracheal cartilage. Nothing.

Your Yorkie's tracheal rings were slowly flattening. And no cough suppressant in the world was going to change that.

data.caption: trycanislabs.com
data.copy:
Three dogs were euthanized last month after bite incidents.

Same behavioral progression. Same failed interventions. Same outcome.

And all three owners had spent over $8,000 trying to prevent it.

Dr. Sarah Mitchell noticed it first. She pulled me and Dr. James Rodriguez into her office and spread out three files on her desk.

"Look at the timeline."

Every single dog: reactive on walks, lunging escalated to snapping, eventually bit someone.

Every single dog: tried training classes, gentle leaders, basket muzzles, prescription medications.

Every single dog: bloodwork came back "normal" — but the reactivity never stopped getting worse.

Dr. Rodriguez leaned back in his chair. "What if we've been treating the wrong system?"

That question led to a six-month investigation that uncovered something the pet supplement industry has been hiding from veterinarians and dog owners for years.

My name is Dr. Marcus Thompson, DVM. Along with Dr. Sarah Mitchell and Dr. James Rodriguez, we've collectively treated over 28,000 dogs at Westside Animal Hospital.

And here's what we found.

It started with a dog named Bear.

His owner, David, had spent $6,800 on behaviorists, medications, and training. Tried every reactivity protocol on the market. Couldn't walk Bear more than 30 feet without him lunging.

Everything came back normal. But Bear kept getting worse.

Bear was a 4-year-old Belgian Malinois. Perfect weight. No disease history. Fed premium food, exercised daily, given all the supplements we recommended.

But he lunged at every dog. Every person. Every bicycle.

David had tried everything: Private reactivity training, group classes, gentle leaders, front-clip harnesses, basket muzzles.

He'd spent $6,800 on two different veterinary behaviorists and prescription Prozac.

Nothing worked for more than a few days.

Bear was still lunging. Still barking. Still pulling so hard David's shoulder was injured.

Then it got worse.

Bear started snapping. Not making contact yet, but…

data.caption: Ich bin Tierärztin. Ich weigere mich, meinen eigenen Hund auf Verhaltensmedikamente zu setzen.
data.copy:
Nach 14 Jahren in der Tierklinik Berlin sah ich, wie eine Familie ihren 4-jährigen Deutschen Schäferhund zur Verhaltens-Euthanasie abgab.

Der Biss war der dritte in sechs Monaten. Der letzte hatte bei einem 9-Jährigen Haut durchbissen. Mit seiner kollabierenden Auslöserschwelle und seiner Beißakte auf dem Rekord gab es nirgendwo mehr für ihn zu gehen.

Als ich nach Hause kam, wartete Bear an der Tür. Schwanzwedelnd.

Er ist 3. Reaktiv bei jedem Spaziergang. Er riss letzten Dienstag an unserem Nachbarn.

Sein Auslösermuster sieht genau so aus wie das von Atlas.

Mein Name ist Dr. Karen Patel, Tierärztin. Ich habe in meiner Karriere über 1.800 Verhaltenskonsultationen durchgeführt.

Ich wusste, was das Protokoll war. Ich konnte es ihm einfach nicht antun.

Also setzte ich mich um 2 Uhr morgens und begann, nach etwas anderem zu suchen.

Drei Nächte später fand ich eine Entdeckung, die alles in Frage stellte, was mir im Tiermedizinstudium je beigebracht worden war — und warum die Branche nie wollte, dass ich frage.

Hier ist, was passierte.

Atlas war ein 4-Jähriger mit einem dieser großen, intelligenten Deutschen Schäferhund-Gesichter.

Seine Besitzerin Maria hatte alles versucht, um diesen Tag zu vermeiden. Sie hatte 4.200 € für drei separate reaktive Hunde-Trainer ausgegeben — fuhr jeweils 90 Minuten einfache Strecke zu Spezialisten. Versuchte Prozac, dann Trazodon, dann beides gleichzeitig. Versuchte Gentle Leader, Korbmaulkorb, Kopfhalter. Versuchte fünf verschiedene „Beruhigungs"-Nahrungsergänzungsmittel von ihrem Tierarzt und aus dem Internet.

Sie war die Art von Besitzerin, die wir uns für jeden Klienten wünschen.

Und sie hatte alles richtig gemacht.

Also machten wir jede Verhaltensbeurteilung, die ich hatte. Blutwerte, Schilddrüsenpanel, vollständiges neurologisches Screening. Drei Termine. Je zwei Stunden.

Hier ist, was niemand dir über einen Hund mit eskalierender Reaktivität sagt:

Du bittest ein Gehirn, das seit Jahren …

data.caption: 83% of cats on premium food had this deficiency
data.copy:
Three cats died at Animal Care Veterinary Clinic last month.

Same symptoms. Same age range. Same test results.

And all three owners had spent over $12,000 trying to save them.

Dr. Park noticed it first. He pulled me and Dr. Chen into his office and spread out three files on his desk.

"Look at the food history."

Every single cat: premium grain-free diet. The exact brands we'd been recommending for years.

Every single cat: chronic vomiting for 6-18 months before the crisis.

Every single cat: "normal" bloodwork until the day their heart started failing.

Dr. Chen leaned back in her chair. "What if we've been missing something?"

That question led to a six-month investigation that uncovered something the pet food industry has been hiding from veterinarians and cat owners for decades.

My name is Dr. Marcus Smith, DVM. Along with Dr. Marcus Chen and Dr. James Park, we've collectively treated over 34,000 cats at Animal Care Veterinary Clinic.

And here's what we found.

It started with a cat named Whiskers.

His owner, Barbara, had spent $3,200 on tests. Tried six different foods. Cleaned up vomit every morning for eight months.

Everything came back normal. But Whiskers kept throwing up.

Whiskers was nine years old. Perfect weight. No disease history. Fed a leading grain-free premium brand - the exact $80-per-bag food we'd all been recommending for years.

But he was vomiting 4-5 times per week. Always undigested food. Sometimes just bile.

She'd tried every "sensitive stomach" formula on the market. Spent $3,200 on GI workups, ultrasounds, endoscopies.

Everything came back normal.

But Whiskers kept throwing up.

She couldn't watch him suffer anymore. And she couldn't afford another round of specialist visits that wouldn't find anything anyway.

So she started filling out the shelter surrender form.

keyword.description: Free-text search string (lowercased server-side). Use for product names, brands, hooks, domains — not for category/niche (use niches).
keyword.allowed_values: Any string; empty = no text filter.

searchkeyword.description: Which ad field keyword searches. NOT a niche/category selector.
searchkeyword.allowed_values: All, landingurl, pagename, adtext, productname. Default All when keyword is set.

countries.description: Ad target countries (where the ad runs — wlads.countries). Not store HQ.
countries.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.
countries.notes: MX/CO/CL are not in this Meta targeting catalog. Use store_based_in for stores based in those markets.

excludeCountries.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.

storebasedin.description: Store Based In (dashboard storebasedin → store_traffic.shop_origin_country). Use for Mexico/Colombia/Chile/etc. store HQ.
storebasedin.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2 including MX, CO, CL, AR, PE and other Explore Shops Based In markets.

niches.description: Product category / vertical filter (dashboard Meta niches). Use when user asks for a category, niche, vertical, or market — not keyword.
niches.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: CG, AM, GG, JY, GS, HT, BY, BG, SK, WC, MC, SP, KS, TS, HE, PS, DP, HI, FT, OG, OP, TR, AC, AA, BM, FK, SH, SW, EL, FW, WT, EW, FR, GM, PH, EC, WE, SC, BE, MU, PA, CB, CF, CP, DC, CT, HH, SG, YG, CC, PZ, LS, GP, WN, SF, OR, MG, PB. See allowed_niches in response for code→label map. Fashion/clothing = CG.

website.description: Detected store/checkout technology on the landing page (dashboard Website filter).
website.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: SH, TP, BU, LS, CC, SL, TA, GG, FU, CS, LP, FO, SI, GP, XS, YC, HY, DI, MS, SB, PP, WC, TT, TW, PI, GO, SC, FB, MG, WP, SQ, PS, GM, KV, CO, HJ, WX, AR, BC, MC. SH=Shopify, WC=WooCommerce, CS=Clickfunnels. See allowed_technologies in response.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
